subject: Culture
title: Shikoku 88 Temples
description: A quick win: understand Shikoku 88 Temples.

hook.text: Japan's Shikoku pilgrimage loops past 88 Buddhist temples over 1,200 km. Walkers wear white as if already dead.

buildup.text: The route follows the footsteps of Kūkai, an 8th-century monk who founded Shingon Buddhism.

discovery.text: Pilgrims walk in pairs—themselves and the spirit of Kūkai. Staffs are inscribed 'We two walk together.'

twist.text: Modern pilgrims include atheists and tourists. The route's power comes from the walking, not the doctrine.

climax.text: Local villagers offer free food and lodging to pilgrims—a tradition called 'osettai' that's lasted centuries.

punchline.text: The kindness of strangers is the real temple.

quiz.question: Who founded the Shikoku pilgrimage tradition?

details.summary: The Shikoku 88 Temple Pilgrimage is a 1,200-kilometer Buddhist circuit around Japan's smallest main island, visiting 88 temples associated with the monk Kūkai. Walking the entire route takes 30-60 days.
details.whyItMatters: Shikoku's pilgrimage demonstrates how circular routes — ending where they began — embody spiritual teachings about cycles, impermanence, and the journey being more important than the destination.
takeaways: The full circuit covers 1,200 km and takes 30-60 days on foot
Pilgrims wear white and carry staffs representing the monk Kūkai
The circular route symbolizes the Buddhist cycle of birth and rebirth

faq.question: Who was Kūkai and why is he important?
faq.answer: Kūkai (774-835 CE) was a Japanese Buddhist monk who founded Shingon Buddhism and is believed to have trained at the 88 temple sites on Shikoku. He is one of Japan's most revered religious figures.

faq.question: Can anyone do the Shikoku pilgrimage?
faq.answer: Yes. The pilgrimage is open to anyone regardless of religion. While traditionally walked, modern pilgrims also use buses, cars, or bicycles. Local communities along the route practice osettai — giving gifts of food, drink, or lodging to pilgrims as a form of merit-making.
